title: China Doubles Down on Legacy Chips as Anthropic Accuses Chinese AI Firms of Abuse
subhead: Beijing's state funds pour money into older-node fabs and a US AI lab claims Chinese firms secretly routed traffic through Claude, sharpening the split between the two countries' AI stacks.

sections.heading: Beijing's State Funds Back Hua Hong as Optical Chip Stocks Slide
sections.body:
Chinese state investors are increasing support for contract chipmaker Hua Hong and backing a new fab in Wuxi, according to SCMP, in a push to strengthen domestic semiconductor supply focused on so-called legacy (mature-node) chips. The move deepens the strategic split: while Washington tries to throttle China's access to leading-edge tools, Beijing is cementing control over the older-generation chips that power cars, appliances, and industrial gear.

At the same time, SCMP reports Chinese optical chip stocks extended a rout on fears of potential new US curbs, with upstream laser-chip suppliers taking the steepest losses. The pattern — state money flowing into the domestic base while export-exposed names sell off — shows how policy risk is now priced directly into Chinese chip equities.

Separately, Chinese AI chipmaker Biren tumbled 12% as it sought US$510 million in a share placement, its second since listing in Hong Kong in January (SCMP).
sections.whyItMatters: China is responding to export controls not by chasing the leading edge it cannot reach, but by locking down the mature-node capacity the rest of the world still depends on — a slower but harder-to-disrupt form of leverage.

sections.heading: Anthropic Says Chinese AI Firms Secretly Used Claude
sections.body:
SCMP reports that Anthropic has claimed Chinese AI firms secretly routed traffic through its Claude models, raising questions about access controls and model security. According to SCMP, if the claims are true, Beijing's main concern would not be intellectual-property theft or model copying but data security — the risk that Chinese firms' queries and data passed through a foreign provider.

The allegation lands amid tightening access rules: earlier this month SCMP reported that Anthropic tightened VPN access to Claude for Hong Kong users, with some users rerouting through Singapore and foreign payment methods to keep access. Anthropic's move and its accusation against Chinese firms mark a shift from competition over capabilities toward policing who can touch whose models.
sections.whyItMatters: As frontier AI models become strategic infrastructure, the fight is moving from who builds the best model to who is allowed to use it — and how cross-border access gets verified.

sections.heading: Subsea Cables Emerge as a Front in the Hybrid War
sections.body:
A new CSIS analysis (October 8) finds that Chinese research vessels spend a statistically significantly larger share of time on the high seas near critical undersea infrastructure than comparable fleets. The study compared over 200 research vessels across 47 nations and concluded that for four of the last five years, PRC research ships ranked in the top 20th percentile of vessels active near critical infrastructure, with a notable increase in 2024.

CSIS notes that undersea fiber-optic cables carry an estimated 99% of international data traffic, supporting daily transactions worth roughly $22.4 trillion. It argues satellite links cannot replace that bandwidth, and that cable repairs can take days to months — making disruption a low-cost way to cause outsized damage.

The report cites the dual-use nature of these civilian vessels, which offer plausible deniability while gathering intelligence and surveillance, and calls for stronger allied monitoring, coordinated patrols, and faster cable repair.
sections.whyItMatters: The undersea cable network is the physical layer of the global internet, and the CSIS data suggests surveillance of it is now routine rather than episodic — a quiet but consequential expansion of gray-zone activity.

sections.heading: AI-Enabled Breaches Leak Data on 320 Million People in a Month
sections.body:
A Nikkei tally found global data breaches leaked personal information for at least 320 million people since September, with at least some cases thought to involve artificial intelligence. Breaches were reported across a broad range of sectors — banks, utilities, and restaurant operators among them.

Nikkei's framing is notable: AI is seen as a factor enabling attackers more than it helps defenders, a gap that widens the asymmetry between offense and defense. The 320 million figure covers only roughly one month of incidents, underscoring how quickly exposed personal data accumulates at scale.
sections.whyItMatters: The offensive advantage of AI in cybersecurity is showing up in the breach numbers, not just in theory — and defenders have yet to convert the same tools into comparable gains.

sections.heading: AI Infrastructure Bets Face a Reality Check: Firmus Pulls $5B IPO
sections.body:
Nvidia-backed data center developer Firmus withdrew its Sydney IPO, Nikkei reports, citing 'recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions.' The company had aimed to raise up to AU$7.9 billion (US$5.5 billion) at AU$11 per share, implying a valuation of about AU$43.9 billion (US$30.7 billion) — which would have made it Australia's second-largest listing after Telstra in 1997.

Fund managers called the offer overpriced. Ron Shamgar of Tamim Asset Management told Nikkei the valuation was 'excessive' at 13 times EBIT for what is essentially a startup with 'a lot of execution risk,' while Red Leaf Securities' John Athanasiou called the AU$44 billion figure 'astronomical.'

Firmus operates two data centers in Australia and Singapore and has five in development across Australia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia. It leases Nvidia-accelerated capacity to customers including OpenAI and Meta, and has raised more than $3 billion privately at a valuation above $10.5 billion, with Nvidia, Coatue, and Blackstone involved.
sections.whyItMatters: After months of AI compute being financed on optimism, a marquee listing has been pulled for being too expensive relative to earnings — a sign investors are becoming selective about AI infrastructure rather than writing blank checks.

sections.heading: Korea's Chip Windfall Funds a National AI Push; Synopsys Courts Chinese Labs
sections.body:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix continue to post record earnings on the AI boom, and South Korea's government is tapping that tax base to reinvest in the country's industrial foundation, Nikkei reports. Recent milestones include Samsung's Q3 profit jumping nearly ninefold in the AI chip boom and President Lee ordering officials to accelerate $589 billion in AI hub plans. South Korea is also moving to curb union leverage over AI and chip windfalls.

On the US side, chip design software leader Synopsys said it is looking to partner with large language model builders in China to help Chinese companies design chips faster using AI versions of its tools, while vowing to work within Washington's tightening export controls (Nikkei). Synopsys forecast $11.15 billion in revenue for FY27, citing AI-driven demand from deals with OpenAI and Amazon.
sections.whyItMatters: Memory-chip profits are being converted into state industrial strategy in Korea, while a top US EDA vendor is testing how far commercial engagement with Chinese AI labs can go inside export-control limits — two different models for capturing the AI boom.

sections.heading: Washington's 'Super Intelligence' Rebrand Sets Off a Domain Land Grab
sections.body:
Registrations for internet domains ending in .si surged worldwide after US President Donald Trump called for artificial intelligence to be rebranded as 'super intelligence,' Nikkei reports, with squatters nabbing thousands of registrations following the order. SCMP reported earlier that Trump's insistence on the term reflects a wider debate over the technology's future trajectory.

The episode is minor on its face, but it illustrates how a single policy signal from Washington can instantly reprice and reorganize naming and branding across the AI sector — and how thin the distinction has become between terminology and market behavior.
sections.whyItMatters: Symbolic policy moves now ripple instantly through digital infrastructure, a reminder that in the AI race, framing and finance move faster than either technology or regulation.

bottomLine: Today crystallized the divergence between the two AI stacks. On one side, Chinese state funds are reinforcing mature-node chip capacity through Hua Hong and a new Wuxi fab, even as optical chip stocks slide on US curb fears and Anthropic accuses Chinese firms of routing traffic through Claude. On the other, Nvidia-backed Firmus pulled its US$5.5 billion Australian IPO over an 'excessive' valuation, while Samsung and SK Hynix's record earnings are being converted into a $589 billion Korean national AI program and Synopsys tests how far it can work with Chinese AI labs under US export rules. Underneath all of it, CSIS data shows Chinese research vessels spending outsized time near the undersea cables that carry 99% of international data, and a Nikkei tally counts 320 million people's data breached in a single month. The through-line is that control is shifting from who builds the best technology to who can access, surveil, and finance it.
sources: SCMP, Nikkei Asia, CSIS, Defense News, Tom's Hardware
